# ALS evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025; this does not remove knowledge already in a model's training. Co-Scientist outputs are not included.

## Research question

Propose one specific, testable hypothesis connecting phosphorylation of a nuclear-pore-complex nucleoporin to ALS-related neuronal dysfunction. Explain the causal chain, distinguish an initiating mechanism from a downstream response, and propose an experimental strategy that discriminates the hypothesis from an alternative. Identify supported premises, speculative bridges, and a falsifying observation. This adapts Co-Scientist Supplementary Note 10; nucleoporin phosphorylation is not supplied as an established ALS cause.

## S1 — TDP-43 and nuclear-pore dysfunction

Chou et al. (2018), *TDP-43 pathology disrupts nuclear pore complexes and nucleocytoplasmic transport in ALS/FTD*. Nature Neuroscience. DOI: `10.1038/s41593-017-0047-3`; PMID: `29311743`; PMCID: `PMC5800968`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29311743/).

Nuclear-pore and transport components were associated with insoluble TDP-43 aggregates. Disease-linked TDP-43 disrupted nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport in experimental cell systems; relevant pore pathology was observed in ALS tissue. This supports examining the connection between TDP-43 pathology and transport disruption. It does not identify a nucleoporin phosphorylation event as the initiating cause or establish the same sequence in every ALS subtype.

## S2 — C9orf72-associated transport defects

Zhang et al. (2015), *The C9orf72 repeat expansion disrupts nucleocytoplasmic transport*. Nature. DOI: `10.1038/nature14973`; PMID: `26308891`; PMCID: `PMC4800742`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26308891/).

Expanded C9orf72 repeat RNA was linked to altered RanGAP localization and impaired nuclear import in models and patient-derived neurons. Manipulations of transport or repeat-RNA-associated mechanisms modified model phenotypes. This supplies a genetic-context-specific route to transport dysfunction. It does not show that sporadic ALS arises by the same route or directly establish a nucleoporin phosphorylation mechanism.

## S3 — A stress-granule-independent route

Gasset-Rosa et al. (2019), *Cytoplasmic TDP-43 De-mixing Independent of Stress Granules Drives Inhibition of Nuclear Import, Loss of Nuclear TDP-43, and Cell Death*. Neuron. DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2019.02.038`; PMID: `30853299`; PMCID: `PMC6548321`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30853299/).

Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies could form independently of conventional stress granules. They recruited or mislocalized transport-associated proteins and were associated with impaired transport, nuclear TDP-43 depletion, and cell death. Phosphorylated TDP-43 accumulated in these assemblies. That is not itself evidence of nucleoporin phosphorylation. The experimental perturbations do not establish that every physiological ALS trajectory begins in this way.

## S4 — A stress-granule-associated route

Zhang et al. (2018), *Stress Granule Assembly Disrupts Nucleocytoplasmic Transport*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2018.03.025`; PMID: `29628143`; PMCID: `PMC6083872`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29628143/).

Cellular stress recruited transport factors into stress granules and impaired nucleocytoplasmic transport. Altering stress-granule assembly modified transport defects and disease-model phenotypes. This provides a sequestration-based alternative to an intrinsic pore-modification hypothesis. Read alongside S3, it does not justify assuming that conventional stress granules are required for every TDP-43-associated transport defect.

## Evidence boundaries

- These selected passages do not establish that nucleoporin phosphorylation initiates ALS. Label a proposed kinase, modification site, or interaction as an assumption unless a supplied source supports it.
- Specify the ALS context; do not assume a universal mechanism across genetic and sporadic disease.
- Distinguish pore alteration, transport-factor sequestration, and failure secondary to broader stress.
- Explain temporal and perturbational evidence that would distinguish cause from consequence.
- Propose a research hypothesis rather than claiming a mechanism or treatment has been validated.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Hypothesis title: Stress-activated phosphorylation of the FG-nucleoporin Nup98 as an initiating lesion in nucleocytoplasmic transport failure in TDP-43-linked ALS motor neurons.

Hypothesis and causal chain. In TDP-43-linked ALS (sporadic disease with TDP-43 proteinopathy and TDP-43-model motor neurons; not assumed for C9orf72 ALS), chronic ALS-relevant stress activates stress kinases that phosphorylate Nup98, an intrinsically disordered FG-repeat nucleoporin of the nuclear pore. Phosphorylation of FG-domain serine/threonine motifs is proposed to weaken the cohesive FG-network forming the pore permeability barrier, slowing Ran-dependent nuclear import. Prolonged import slowing depletes nuclear TDP-43, enabling cytoplasmic TDP-43 de-mixing, which then amplifies transport collapse by recruiting and mislocalizing transport factors. Temporally, phosphorylation is hypothesized to be the initiating lesion; TDP-43 aggregate-associated pore disruption and stress-granule sequestration of transport factors are positioned downstream or in parallel as amplifiers.

Supported premises from the packet.
- TDP-43 pathology associates with insoluble nuclear-pore and transport components and disrupts nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport in cell systems and ALS tissue [S1].
- Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies can form independently of stress granules, recruit or mislocalize transport proteins, and are associated with impaired import, nuclear TDP-43 loss, and cell death [S3].
- Stress recruits transport factors into stress granules and impairs transport; altering stress-granule assembly modifies transport defects and disease-model phenotypes [S4].
- In C9orf72 ALS, repeat RNA perturbs RanGAP localization and import, showing transport failure can be an upstream event in at least one ALS subtype [S2]; this motivates testing upstream pore-intrinsic lesions in the TDP-43 context without generalizing across subtypes.

Speculative bridges (explicit assumptions; not established by the packet).
- Kinase and site: p38 MAPK or JNK acting on Nup98 FG-domain S/TP sites is an assumption. Unverified prior knowledge outside the packet: Nup98 and related FG-nucleoporins are disordered and are phosphorylated during mitotic pore disassembly; whether stress kinases phosphorylate them in post-mitotic neurons is untested.
- Biophysical link: that phosphorylation reduces FG-network cohesion enough to slow physiologic import rates is an assumption.
- Temporal primacy: that phosphorylation precedes nuclear TDP-43 depletion and cytoplasmic aggregation is the central untested claim.

Alternative explanations to discriminate.
1. Sequestration-first model [S4]: stress-granule sequestration of transport factors initiates failure; phosphorylation is a nonspecific stress readout.
2. Aggregate-first model [S1, S3]: cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies mechanically mislocalize or sequester pore components; phosphorylation is secondary.
3. Context model [S2]: C9orf72 repeat-RNA mechanisms drive transport defects independently of nucleoporin phosphorylation.

Discriminating preclinical test strategy.
(a) Order of events: in isogenic iPSC-derived motor neurons (TDP-43-linked ALS line versus CRISPR-corrected control) exposed to graded oxidative stress, quantify Nup98 phosphorylation (phosphoproteomics on enriched pore fractions), Ran-gradient and import-reporter kinetics by live imaging, nuclear TDP-43, and stress-granule formation at matched early time points. Prediction: phosphorylation rises before import slows, before stress-granule sequestration, and before nuclear TDP-43 loss.
(b) Perturbation: CRISPR knock-in phospho-null (S/T-to-A) and phospho-mimetic (S/T-to-D/E) Nup98 alleles at candidate sites. Prediction: phospho-null preserves import and nuclear TDP-43 under stress; phospho-mimetic impairs import without stress and without stress granules.
(c) Alternative discrimination: repeat with stress-granule assembly manipulated as in [S4]. If phospho-null rescues transport despite stress-granule formation, or stress-granule blockade rescues transport while phosphorylation persists, pore-intrinsic initiation is supported; if stress-granule blockade fully rescues and phospho-null is inert, the sequestration model is favored.
(d) Specificity: test phospho-null in C9orf72-repeat models; no effect would support subtype-specific mechanisms [S2].

Falsifying observation. Nup98 phosphorylation appearing only after stress-granule formation and import collapse, or phospho-null alleles failing to protect import and TDP-43 localization while the phospho-mimetic shows normal import, would falsify the initiating-phosphorylation hypothesis and indicate a secondary, sequestration- or aggregation-driven lesion.

Limitations. The candidate kinase and sites are assumptions; functional redundancy among FG-nucleoporins may mask single-site effects and require multi-nucleoporin mutagenesis. Phospho-mimetic substitution imperfectly mimics phosphorylation. iPSC motor neurons are immature relative to adult motor neurons, and acute stress compresses a decades-long disease course, so phosphorylation could be necessary without being sufficient. The packet sources predate 2025 and include no nucleoporin phosphoproteomics in ALS, so this remains a hypothesis, not a validated mechanism [S1-S4].

Ranked proposal:
Stress-activated phosphorylation of the FG-nucleoporin Nup98 as an initiating lesion in nucleocytoplasmic transport failure in TDP-43-linked ALS motor neurons
